title: Diabetes Remission in 90 Days? Doctors Explain What the Term Really Means
excerpt: Remission means an HbA1c below 6.5% held for at least three months without medication — a definition, not a deadline. Doctors explain the weight-loss mechanism, the South Asian risk caveat, and why real-world remission rates are far lower than trial headlines.
body:
• Remission has a strict definition, doctors say: an HbA1c below 6.5%, held for at least three months, with no glucose-lowering medication — so "90 days" is the minimum time needed to prove remission, not a quick-fix programme.
  • Weight loss drives it: doctors cited by OnlyMyHealth say losing 10-15% of body weight can significantly improve the chances of remission, especially soon after diagnosis.
  • In absolute terms, real-world remission is uncommon: in a Thai cohort of 29,706 newly diagnosed patients, 3.44% achieved a first remission within one year and 8.32% within five years — and 38.38% of those who remitted relapsed within a year.
  • Never stop or reduce diabetes medication on your own: as blood sugar improves, doses need a doctor's review, and monitoring continues even after remission.

"Remission in 90 days" is a phrase that invites misunderstanding, and doctors marking World Diabetes Day on November 14 were careful to define their terms. Type 2 diabetes remission is not a cure, and it is not measured in days of dieting. According to the international consensus criteria published in Diabetes Care and cited by physicians interviewed by OnlyMyHealth, remission means an HbA1c below 6.5%, maintained at that level for at least three months, while taking no glucose-lowering medication. HbA1c itself measures average blood glucose over roughly three months — which is why 90 days is the floor for confirming remission, not a promise that it can be achieved on that schedule.

Why weight loss is the mechanism

Excess fat, particularly abdominal fat and fat deposited around internal organs, makes it harder for the body to regulate blood glucose, Prof Dr S. M. Fayaz, lead and senior consultant in internal medicine at KIMS Hospitals, Mahadevapura, explained to OnlyMyHealth. Fat in the liver can increase glucose production, while fat around the pancreas may interfere with insulin-producing cells. Losing that fat reduces the metabolic pressure, improves insulin sensitivity and lowers the burden on the pancreas, the doctors said.

Dr Sabine Kapasi said losing more than 10% of initial body weight can offer significant metabolic benefits in some individuals, and the doctors noted that weight loss of around 10-15% may improve the chances of remission — particularly when diabetes has been diagnosed relatively recently, because more insulin-producing cells may still be functioning.

The South Asian caveat: BMI alone misleads

Dr Alok Krishna Sahay, a senior consultant physician and diabetologist at Prayag Hospitals, added a point of direct relevance to Indian and diaspora readers: even people who appear to be a normal body weight can carry excess abdominal fat, and South Asians may develop metabolic problems at relatively lower BMI levels. Waist circumference, blood glucose and lipid profile are important indicators alongside BMI, he said.

What the absolute numbers look like

Trial results and everyday practice are far apart, and the gap matters more than any single success story. A retrospective cohort study of 29,706 newly diagnosed patients in Thailand, published in BMJ Open, used the same definition — HbA1c below 6.5% for at least 90 days after stopping glucose-lowering medication. In that real-world setting, the probability of a first remission was 3.44% at one year and 8.32% at five years. Remission was also frequently temporary: 38.38% of patients who achieved it relapsed within one year. The study's authors note that randomised trials of intensive lifestyle interventions have reported far higher one-year remission rates — roughly 40% to 80% among adherent participants — which is precisely why a percentage quoted without its setting should be read with care. Remission, when achieved, was associated with a significantly lower incidence of cardiorenal outcomes in the cohort.

Our coverage of an Indian study published this week makes the same distinction from the other direction: a structured programme of traditional food and daily walking put an estimated 61% of early-diagnosis participants into remission over six months — a trial result, in a selected group, not a general rate. Read it here: Traditional Indian Diet and Daily Walks Put 61% of Early Diabetes Patients in Remission, Study Finds.

What doctors say to do — and not do

Dr Sahay recommends reducing refined carbohydrates, controlling portion sizes and building regular physical activity into everyday routines, with a balanced diet of adequate protein, fibre-rich foods, vegetables and healthy fats. Dr Kapasi cautions against drastic dieting, prolonged fasting or stopping prescribed medicines without medical advice, which can cause complications and make glucose control harder. Dr Sahay emphasised that remission requires medical supervision: as blood glucose improves with weight loss, medication may need to be reviewed and adjusted by a doctor, and patients should never reduce or stop prescribed medicines independently. Monitoring continues after remission, because diabetes can return, particularly if weight is regained.

For readers in the United States with prediabetes rather than diabetes, the CDC's National Diabetes Prevention Program is the established, structured route — its lifestyle programme targets a 5-7% weight loss, as set out in the CDC programme materials. For anyone already diagnosed, the first step is a conversation with their own doctor about whether remission is a realistic goal in their case — not a 90-day deadline.
